A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GCN retrieval and multi-head early-exit framework for CTR prediction. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: Section 6, Tables 2–4 and Appendix Figures 3–5 report original recommendation, throughput, ablation and sensitivity results on three datasets.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices A.3–A.4 report original five-dataset evaluations, component ablations, efficiency comparisons and sensitivity results.

M1.justification: Exit heads change from random initialization in v1 Section 5.2 to initialization from the existing LLM head in v2 Section 5.2 and Algorithm 2. The main architecture and staged training remain. Algorithm 2 newly specifies probability ratios, but conflicts with v2's probability-difference equations, so a further scoring-method revision is not securely established.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from BookCrossing, Amazon Beauty and Video Games to include Amazon Movies and TV and Yelp. Tables 1–2 establish actual evaluation in these additional movie and business-review domains while retaining the binary recommendation task.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds AutoInt, DCNv2, WuKong, GDCN and EulerNet and removes SIM. v2 also evaluates FM retrieval, SparseGPT, TinyLlama and a single-head exit variant in Tables 4–5 and 9, substantially expanding the comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds log loss, changes the reported Video Games sample count from 294,135 to 221,465, and extends BookCrossing's designated exit layers through layer 30 instead of 20. New evaluation settings include 50% projection-layer sparsity for SparseGPT, adaptive-learning-rate controls and a zero-example point in the retrieval sensitivity sweep.

E4.justification: v2 adds weighted versus average/final-layer aggregation, single-head versus multi-head exiting, and adaptive-learning-rate ablations in Tables 3–4 and Figure 4. Threshold, window and retrieval-example sensitivity tests already existed in v1's appendix; v2 Figure 6 substantially revises their evidence and extends them to five datasets.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The expanded results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Many AUC and throughput entries change, alongside new dataset, comparator and log-loss results. For example, Table 2 reports BookCrossing full-model AUC as 73.28 in v1 and 82.11 in v2; its reported retrieval speedup changes from 7.15x to 1.4x in the corresponding figures. These are revised results, not established same-setting improvements. Appendix sensitivity plots also change from mostly modest threshold/window effects to pronounced accuracy losses.

T1.justification: The window-mean equation changes from summing m+1 terms in v1 Section 5.3 to m terms in v2 Section 5.1 while retaining division by m. This is a limited mathematical correction; no theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims that GCN retrieval and multi-head early exit accelerate recommendation while preserving or improving CTR accuracy. Naming the framework OptiRAG-Rec and expanding its evaluation do not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving graph topology, head specialization, retrieval–exit synergy and compression trade-offs. Its limitations expand beyond textual metadata to cold-start users, training cost, domain transfer and missing real-time graph updates. Appendix A.4 also interprets newly reported failures at larger exit thresholds and windows.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset-specific prompt templates and two pseudocode algorithms, plus GCN depth and embedding size, default exit settings and SparseGPT pruning details. These substantially expand implementation documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed setting changed. Conversely, v1's BookCrossing-specific target sampling and rating-threshold description is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 expands its positioning through an introductory comparison with quantization and speculative decoding and an appendix contrasting dynamic exiting with pruning and model compression. It adds literature for these alternatives, FM retrieval and the expanded CTR baselines. Some attribution is problematic: the introductory Kangaroo citation points to a video-language paper in v2's reference list.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and method/experiment narrative, consolidates preliminaries in Section 3, and reverses the order of exit workflow and head optimization. Experiments are reorganized around six questions, the framework receives a consistent name, and the brief appendix becomes structured subsections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a branded single-column layout. The framework diagram is redrawn, new exit-example and analysis figures appear, and tables are expanded and restructured. v1's three appendix sensitivity figures become v2 Figure 6, whose numerous small panels reduce readability at normal page scale.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's limited evaluation and implementation documentation with broader comparisons, ablations and detailed prompts. However, important new evidence is internally inconsistent: BookCrossing retriever AUC is 72.83 in Table 2 but 78.03 in Table 4, and Movies and TV full-model log loss is 0.3010 in Table 2 but 0.1911 in Table 9. The exit pseudocode also conflicts with the main equations. These unresolved reliability issues prevent confidently determining whether the substantial additions produce a net quality improvement.
